title: Marker Isolation: Does Conversational Structure Survive Without Turn Markers?
hypothesis: The 13% SORC increase observed in exp_004 (multi_turn vs expert) is driven by conversational relational structure, not by the Q:/A: turn markers themselves. If the increase persists when markers are removed, conversational structure is the active variable. If it disappears, the markers were driving token-type diversity independently of relational structure.
prediction: multi_turn_unmarked (no markers) > expert (single paragraph) at matched token count
confound_being_tested: Q:/A: tokens in exp_004 multi_turn contexts inject token-type diversity at regular intervals independent of relational structure. This experiment isolates that effect by using identical conversational content with markers stripped.
context_version: v5 (multi_turn_unmarked: same content as multi_turn, Q:/A: markers removed, flowing prose)
finding: multi_turn_unmarked (183 tok, 0.1530) > expert (206 tok, 0.1406). 8.8% increase, Cohen's d=1.83. Marker contribution to the expert-to-multi_turn gap: (0.1589-0.1530)/(0.1589-0.1406) = 0.0059/0.0183 = 32%. Removing markers reduces the elevation from 13% to 8.8% — markers amplify the effect but do not produce it. The 8.8% elevation over expert persists without markers (d=1.83, large effect). Conversational structure is the driver. Late/early ratio: unmarked 0.637 vs expert 0.626 — both directions consistent with cross-turn structure preserving activation geometry at deep layers.
conclusion: The ISC conversational prediction is supported across two controlled experiments. Conversational structure — question-and-answer alternation covering multiple angles on a domain — produces measurably higher SORC than single-paragraph expert text at matched token count. The effect survives marker removal. This is the first clean empirical evidence that contextual structure, independent of content, affects hidden state geometry in a pre-trained transformer.
